content: Red Alder (Alnus rubra) is a deciduous tree native to the western regions of North America, ranging from southeastern Alaska to central coastal California. It is typically found within 200 kilometers of the Pacific coast, with an inland extension of up to 600 kilometers across northern Washington into northern Idaho. This species is the largest of all alders globally, capable of reaching heights between 20 and 35 meters. The tallest officially recorded Red Alder, measured in 1979, stands at 32 meters in Clatsop County, Oregon, USA. The tree derives its name from the bright rusty-red coloration that appears on its bark when bruised or scraped. The leaves of the Red Alder are ovate, measuring 7 to 15 centimeters in length, with bluntly serrated edges and a distinct pointed tip. In autumn, the leaves turn yellow before falling. The bark is ashy-gray, smooth, and often covered with moss. Male flowers appear as dangling reddish catkins, 10 to 15 centimeters long, in early spring, while female flowers are erect catkins that develop into small, woody, cone-like dry fruits measuring 2 to 3 centimeters in length. The seeds are housed between the woody bracts of these cones and are dispersed during autumn and winter. In the northwestern Coast Ranges of the USA, Red Alder thrives on cool, moist slopes. Further inland and at the southernmost parts of its range, such as in California, it predominantly grows along streams and in swampy areas. It is commonly associated with forests containing Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), Western Hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla), Grand Fir (Abies grandis), Western Redcedar (Thuja plicata), and Sitka Spruce (Picea sitchensis). Other associated species include Red Osier Dogwood (Cornus stolonifera), Oregon Ash (Fraxinus latifolia), and Bigleaf Maple (Acer macrophyllum). In higher mountain regions, it is replaced by the smaller Sitka Alder (Alnus viridis subsp. sinuata), and east of the Cascade Mountains, by Thinleaf Alder (Alnus incana subsp. tenuifolia). Red Alder is a pioneer species in moist forest areas, quickly colonizing burned or clear-cut landscapes. While it temporarily inhibits the growth of conifers, it enhances soil fertility, benefiting future conifer growth. It is a prolific seed producer, but its seeds require open areas of mineral soil to germinate, making disturbed areas such as skid trails or logging sites ideal for seedling establishment. These areas can host hundreds of thousands to millions of seedlings per hectare in the first year following disturbance. Wildlife, including deer and elk, browse on the twigs and buds of Red Alder, particularly in fall, winter, and spring. Beavers consume the bark, while finches such as the Common Redpoll and Pine Siskin, as well as deer mice, feed on the seeds. Additionally, Red Alder plays a crucial ecological role by hosting the nitrogen-fixing actinomycete Frankia, enabling it to thrive in nitrate-poor soils. Historically, Native Americans used a russet dye derived from a decoction of Red Alder bark to dye fishing nets, making them less visible underwater. The tree is also significant in forestry due to its rapid growth, which makes it useful for covering disturbed lands, such as mine spoils. Its fallen leaves decompose readily, forming nitrogen-enriched humus. Red Alder is being considered as a rotation crop to suppress the conifer root pathogen Phellinus weirii (Laminated Root Rot). Despite its past designation as a trash tree by the timber industry, its value has increased due to its benefits to other tree species and its wood's utility. Herbicide spraying of Red Alder in coastal Oregon and Washington has led to lawsuits alleging health issues, including birth defects, but this practice has largely ceased due to the tree's rising value and ecological importance. The wood of Red Alder is not durable for outdoor use but is highly valued for furniture and cabinetry due to its workability and ease of finishing. It ranges in color from white to pinkish to light brown, is relatively soft, and has a medium luster. It is easy to work with, glues well, and takes a good finish. While not commonly planted as an ornamental tree, Red Alder thrives in wet swales or along stream banks. However, it should be planted away from drainage, sewage, and water lines, as its roots can invade and clog these systems. Red Alder is also renowned for its ability to grow readily on burned or disturbed land, making it a valuable pioneering or reclamation tree.
